thomas.t: Apostle of India, Father in faith of the St Thomas Christians
word: Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.”
John 20:29
life: Thomas, called Didymus (“the Twin”), was one of the Twelve chosen by Jesus. The Gospel of John gives us three short scenes that show his character: his courage when Jesus decides to go back to Judea, where his enemies wanted to kill him; his honest question at the Last Supper about the way; and his doubt and great confession after the Resurrection.

Eight days after Easter, the risen Jesus showed Thomas his wounds. Thomas answered with the clearest confession of faith in the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!” He who had doubted became the one who proclaimed Jesus as God.

According to the ancient and constant tradition of the Church in India, Thomas reached the Malabar coast, traditionally at Kodungallur (Muziris) in AD 52, preached the Gospel and founded Christian communities, remembered as the seven and a half churches. He is said to have been martyred by a spear near Mylapore (Chennai) around AD 72; his tomb is venerated in the San Thome Basilica. Part of his relics are kept at Ortona in Italy. The St Thomas Christians of Kerala, Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara, keep his feast, Dukrana, on 3 July.
lessons: Honest questions can lead to deep faith
Thomas did not pretend to understand. He asked, and Jesus answered him with “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
Doubt is not the end
Thomas doubted, but he stayed with the community; on the eighth day he was with the other disciples, and there he met the risen Lord.
Faith is a personal confession
“My Lord and my God” is not a general statement. It is personal: my Lord, my God. Say it at the elevation of the Host.
Faith becomes mission
The apostle who once doubted travelled to the end of the known world. Our faith in Kerala is the fruit of his courage.
stories: “Let us also go, that we may die with him”

When Lazarus died, Jesus decided to return to Judea, though the leaders there wanted to stone him. The other disciples hesitated; Thomas said to them, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 11:16). The one remembered as the doubter was first a man of courage.

An ancient writing, the Acts of Thomas (3rd century), tells that King Gundaphorus gave Thomas money to build him a palace. Thomas gave it all to the poor, and told the king that his palace was being built in heaven. The book is not part of Scripture and the story is legendary, though a king named Gondophares is known from coins of that period.
quotes: Let us also go, that we may die with him.
St Thomas, John 11:16
Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?
St Thomas, John 14:5
My Lord and my God!
St Thomas, John 20:28
The disbelief of Thomas has done more for our faith than the faith of the other disciples.
St Gregory the Great, Homily 26 on the Gospels
thomas.prayer: Lord God, you gave St Thomas the grace to confess your Son as Lord and God. Through his prayers keep alive the faith he planted in our land, and make us, like him, witnesses of the risen Christ. Amen.

points: Let us also go, that we may die with Him (John 11:16): Thomas was ready to follow Jesus into danger.
Lord, how can we know the way? (John 14:5). Honest questions lead to Jesus, the Way.
My Lord and my God (John 20:28): the clearest confession of Christ's divinity in the Gospels.
According to the ancient tradition of the Church in India, Thomas preached here and died a martyr. His faith is our inheritance.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, we often call him doubting Thomas, but the Gospel of John shows us a much richer man. When Jesus decided to return to Judea, where His enemies wanted to kill Him, it was Thomas who said to the others: let us also go, that we may die with Him (John 11:16). He was brave and loyal.

At the Last Supper, when Jesus spoke of going to prepare a place, Thomas asked honestly: Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way? And Jesus gave one of His greatest answers: I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:5–6). Honest questions are not the enemy of faith; brought to Jesus, they lead to deeper faith.

After the Resurrection, Thomas was absent, and he refused to believe without seeing. Eight days later Jesus came again and invited him to touch His wounds. Thomas did not need to touch; he fell down and said: my Lord and my God (John 20:28). The one who doubted made the highest confession in the Gospels. Jesus added a blessing for us: blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe (John 20:29).

According to the ancient and constant tradition of the Church in India, Thomas brought this faith to our land, founded communities and gave his life as a martyr. Let us honour him by living his faith: courageous, honest, adoring and missionary. At every {Q}, when the Body of Christ is raised, let us say with him: my Lord and my God.

opts.a: In the light of the Word: blessed are those who have not seen
points: The risen Christ keeps His wounds (John 20:27; Isaiah 53:5).
The risen Lord's first gift is peace and the Spirit (John 20:19–23).
As the Father has sent me, so I send you (John 20:21).
homily: Dear friends, when Jesus said to Thomas: blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe (John 20:29), He was thinking of us. We have not touched His wounds or seen Him with our eyes. Yet we believe, because of the witness of Thomas and the apostles. That blessing is for every Christian in every age.

Notice that the risen Jesus still bears His wounds. Isaiah had said: by His bruises we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). Jesus did not hide His wounds; He showed them. They became the proof of His love and the place where Thomas found faith. Our wounds too, when we bring them to Christ, can become places of healing and faith.

The first words of the risen Lord to the disciples were: peace be with you. Then He breathed on them and gave them the Holy Spirit and the power to forgive sins (John 20:19–23). Thomas missed that first evening because he was not with the community. Faith grows in the community of the Church, especially on the Lord's Day.

Finally Jesus said: as the Father has sent me, so I send you (John 20:21). Thomas was sent to the ends of the earth. We are sent to our homes, schools and workplaces. Let us not keep our faith to ourselves. Let us say with our words and lives: my Lord and my God.

opts.a: For young people and families: questions and courage
points: God is not afraid of our questions; bring them to Him and to the Church.
Thomas missed Jesus because he was absent; do not skip Sunday.
Let us also go: loyalty to Jesus when it costs something.
My Lord and my God: make the faith of your parents your own.
homily: Dear young people, St Thomas is a saint for you. He was not satisfied with easy answers. He asked questions. Many of you have questions about God, the Church, suffering, science and faith. That is good. God is not afraid of your questions. Bring them to Him in prayer, read the Gospel, ask your parents, your catechist, your priest.

But notice one thing: Thomas missed the first appearance of the risen Jesus because he was not with the others. When we stay away from the community, from Sunday {Q} and from the parish, our questions can become bitterness. Stay close. A week later, when Thomas was with the others, Jesus came to him.

Thomas also had courage. When following Jesus was dangerous, he said: let us also go, that we may die with Him. Today following Jesus may cost you popularity, a party, a lie you will not tell, a friend group you leave. Be loyal like Thomas.

Parents, your children will not inherit faith like land or gold. Each one must make the confession of Thomas personally: my Lord and my God. Pray with them, answer their questions patiently, and live the faith joyfully. Then the faith Thomas brought to our land will pass to the next generation.

alphonsa.n: St Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception
alphonsa.t: Franciscan Clarist sister, first woman saint of India
word: I am now rejoicing in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am completing what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church.
Colossians 1:24
life: Anna Muttathupadathu was born on 19 August 1910 at Kudamaloor near Kottayam. Her mother died when she was a baby, and she was brought up by relatives, in particular a strict aunt. From childhood she loved prayer and wished to belong to Jesus alone.

When a marriage was being arranged for her, she put her foot into a pit of burning chaff, and the injury left her lame for a time; she later explained that she wanted to remain free for God. She joined the Franciscan Clarist Congregation at Bharananganam, took the name Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception, and made her final profession in 1936.

Her religious life was marked by almost constant illness: fevers, pain, a period of memory loss, and weakness. She taught children for a short time, but most of her life was hidden suffering, accepted with a smile and offered for others. She died on 28 July 1946, aged 35. Pope St John Paul II beatified her at Kottayam on 8 February 1986, and Pope Benedict XVI canonised her on 12 October 2008, the first woman saint of India. Her tomb at Bharananganam draws pilgrims of every religion.
lessons: Suffering can become love
Alphonsa did not seek suffering for its own sake. She united her pain to the Cross of Christ and offered it for others.
Holiness in hidden places
She did no great public work. Holiness grew in a small convent, a sick bed and a classroom.
A smile is a gift
Those who lived with her remembered her patience and cheerful face even in pain.
Belonging to Jesus
From childhood she wanted Jesus alone. Every vocation, married or consecrated, begins with that desire.
stories: As a young girl, to avoid a marriage being arranged against her desire, Anna stepped into a pit of smouldering chaff. The burns were serious. It is told in all her biographies; the Church does not propose such acts for imitation, but it shows how completely she wanted to belong to God.
The miracle accepted for her canonisation was the healing of a young boy's deformed feet after prayer at her intercession.
alphonsa.prayer: O God, you gave St Alphonsa the grace to love you in suffering and to serve you with a smile. Through her prayers, help the sick and the suffering to unite their pain to the Cross of Christ, and teach us patience and joy. Amen.

points: From childhood Anna wanted to be wholly God's; she chose religious life at great cost.
Years of illness united to Christ's Cross (Colossians 1:24).
A simple sister in a small convent became the first woman saint of India.
She hid her pain and comforted others, especially children.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, St Alphonsa lived only thirty-six years, almost all of them in a small corner of Kerala. She did not found a congregation, write books or travel. Yet the whole Church honours her as the first woman saint of India. Why?

From childhood Anna Muttathupadathu wanted to belong to Jesus alone. When a marriage was being arranged against her desire, she put her foot into burning chaff, and was injured; she later said she wanted to remain free for God. We are not asked to imitate that act, but to admire her undivided love.

As a Franciscan Clarist sister at Bharananganam she suffered almost constant illness. Instead of becoming bitter, she united her sufferings to the Cross of Christ, like St Paul who rejoiced in his sufferings for the sake of the Church (Colossians 1:24). She prayed for others and offered her pain for them. She hid her suffering behind a smile, and children loved her.

Alphonsa teaches us that holiness is possible in hidden places: in a sickbed, a kitchen, a classroom, a hospital ward. Pain is not wasted when it is offered with love. Let us bring to this {Q} all who suffer, and ask St Alphonsa to teach us to love Jesus in good days and bad.

opts.a: In the light of the Word: completing what is lacking
points: I complete what is lacking in Christ's afflictions (Colossians 1:24).
What is lacking is our share, offered in union with Him.
Unless a grain falls into the earth and dies (John 12:24).
Not loving pain, but loving Christ in pain.
homily: Dear friends, the word chosen for St Alphonsa is from St Paul: I am now rejoicing in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am completing what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of His body, the Church (Colossians 1:24). What can be lacking in the sufferings of Christ? His sacrifice is perfect and complete.

What is lacking is our participation. Christ wants to share His saving work with His members. When a Christian offers his or her suffering in union with Christ, it becomes a channel of grace for others. This is what Alphonsa understood. Her illnesses were not meaningless. She offered them for sinners, for the Church, for the people who came to her for prayer.

Jesus said: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). Alphonsa's short life fell into the earth at Bharananganam. Today her tomb draws pilgrims of every religion, and many receive comfort and grace.

Paul speaks of joy in suffering. Saints do not love pain for itself. They love Christ, and they find Him even in pain. If you are suffering in body or mind, do not waste your suffering in complaint alone. Offer it to God with the simple prayer: Jesus, I offer this for love of you and for those who need grace.

opts.a: For young people and families: the courage to be different
points: Alphonsa knew her heart's desire early.
Do not be crushed by hardship
She lost her mother young and lived under strict care, yet grew in love.
She smiled at others even when she was in pain.
Care for the sick at home
Families meet Christ in their sick members.
homily: Dear young people, St Alphonsa was once a girl like many of you. She lost her mother as a baby and grew up under a strict aunt. Life was not easy. Yet she did not become bitter. She discovered early what her heart wanted most: to belong to Jesus.

Many young people today do not know what they want. They follow the crowd, the screen, the latest trend. Alphonsa had the courage to be different. Ask God every day: Lord, what do you want me to do with my life? And be brave enough to follow His answer.

As a sister she was often ill, but she kept a gentle smile and cared about others. Children loved to be near her. When you are tired, sick or sad, it is easy to be irritable at home. Try Alphonsa's way: one kind word, one smile, offered for love of Jesus.

Families, many of you have a sick or elderly person at home. Caring for them is hard. St Alphonsa reminds us that Christ is present in the sick. Be patient with them, pray with them, bring them Holy Communion. Every act of care in your home can become a prayer.

chavara.t: Priest, founder, reformer of the Church in Kerala
word: In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.
Matthew 5:16
life: Kuriakose Chavara was born on 10 February 1805 at Kainakary near Alappuzha and was ordained a priest in 1829. With Fr Thomas Palackal and Fr Thomas Porukara he founded at Mannanam (1831) the first indigenous religious congregation for men in India, today the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate (CMI). He took the name Kuriakose Elias of the Holy Family and became its first Prior General.

He was a great reformer. He started a printing press at Mannanam, encouraged a school beside every church, began houses for the poor and the dying, renewed the liturgy and the retreats of the people, and with the Carmelite missionary Fr Leopold Beccaro founded in 1866 the first congregation of sisters of the Syro-Malabar Church, today the Congregation of the Mother of Carmel (CMC). As Vicar General, he defended the unity of the Church with the Holy See during the Rochos crisis of 1861.

He wrote poems, spiritual works and a famous testament to Christian families, the Chavarul. He died at Koonammavu on 3 January 1871. He was beatified at Kottayam on 8 February 1986 and canonised by Pope Francis on 23 November 2014.
lessons: Holiness and service go together
Chavara's prayer produced schools, a press, homes for the poor and new religious communities.
Education is a work of faith
His call for a school beside every church shaped the literacy of Kerala.
Love for the unity of the Church
In a time of division he chose fidelity to the Successor of Peter.
The family is a school of heaven
His Chavarul gives simple, practical advice for parents and children.
stories: Chavara encouraged parishes to open a school next to the church, so that poor children, of every caste and community, could learn to read. Many Kerala schools trace their origin to this movement.

Before he died he wrote a letter of counsel to the families of his home parish at Kainakary, the Chavarul. It speaks of prayer, work, honesty, hospitality and the education of children, and is still read in Kerala homes.
quotes: A good Christian family is the image of heaven.
St Kuriakose Elias Chavara, Chavarul (Testament of a Loving Father), in translation
The day on which you have not done any good to others will not be counted in the book of your life.
St Kuriakose Elias Chavara, Chavarul, in translation
chavara.prayer: Lord God, you made St Kuriakose Elias Chavara a man of prayer, a builder of the Church and a teacher of families. Through his intercession make our homes images of heaven and our parishes places of learning and charity. Amen.

points: Ordained in 1829, he lived for his people.
CMI congregation (1831), CMC with Fr Leopold Beccaro (1866), printing press, schools, care for the dying.
Education as a work of faith for every child.
A good Christian family is heaven
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, St Kuriakose Elias Chavara lived in the nineteenth century, a time of change and difficulty for the Church in Kerala. He was a priest, a religious founder, a teacher and a reformer, and he did everything out of love for God and for his people.

With two fellow priests he founded at Mannanam the first indigenous religious congregation for men in India, today the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate. Later, with the Carmelite missionary Fr Leopold Beccaro, he founded a congregation of sisters, today the Congregation of the Mother of Carmel. He started a printing press, encouraged a school beside every church, opened houses for the poor and the dying, and worked for the unity of the Church in difficult times.

His desire for a school beside every church changed Kerala. He understood that faith and education go together, and that every child, of every caste and background, deserved to learn. Today our schools are fruit of that vision. Teachers, you continue his work.

Before his death he wrote a testament to families, saying that a good Christian family is the image of heaven. Let us take this to heart: pray together, raise children with love and discipline, care for the poor. And let us ask St Chavara to help us let our light shine so that others may glorify our Father in heaven (Matthew 5:16).

opts.a: In the light of the Word: let your light shine
points: You are the light of the world (Matthew 5:14).
Good works that point to God
So that they may glorify your Father (Matthew 5:16).
Faith is not hidden under a basket (Matthew 5:15).
Chavara's reforms in a difficult age.
homily: Dear friends, Jesus said to His disciples: you are the light of the world; let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven (Matthew 5:14–16). St Chavara lived this Word.

His good works were many: schools, a press, houses for the destitute, renewal of prayer and liturgy. But notice the purpose Jesus gives: so that people may glorify the Father. Chavara did not seek his own glory. Everything he did pointed to God. His congregation took the name of Mary Immaculate, and he took the name of the Holy Family.

A lamp is not lit to be hidden under a basket. Faith is personal, but never private. Chavara brought the light of faith into education, the press and social care. Christians today must bring that light into politics, business, media and technology, with honesty and service.

Chavara lived in difficult times, with confusion and division in the Church. He did not curse the darkness; he lit lamps. In our own time of difficulty, let us not only complain. Let us light one lamp: help a poor child study, reconcile a quarrel, pray for unity. That is how saints change history.

opts.a: For young people and families: a good family is heaven
points: His schools say: learn well, to serve.
The rosary and evening prayer in his testament.
homily: Dear young people and families, St Chavara cared especially about two things: schools and families. He wanted a school beside every church so that every child could learn, and he wrote a famous testament with advice for families.

Young people, your study is not only for marks or a job. Chavara saw learning as a way to serve God and society. Study honestly, help classmates who struggle, respect your teachers. If you have opportunities that your grandparents never had, use them to serve.

Parents, Chavara said that a good Christian family is the image of heaven. That does not mean a perfect family. It means a family where God is at the centre: evening prayer, Sunday {Q}, forgiveness, discipline with love, and care for elderly parents. Do not let the phone or television take the place of family prayer.

Finally, Chavara opened houses for the poor and the dying. A family that is closed on itself is not yet heaven. Let your family do one good work together this month: visit a sick neighbour, help a poor student, share food. Then your home will be a little heaven, as Chavara hoped.

euphrasia.n: St Euphrasia of the Sacred Heart of Jesus
word: Then Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray always and not to lose heart.
Luke 18:1
life: Rosa Eluvathingal was born on 17 October 1877 at Kattoor near Irinjalakuda, in the diocese of Thrissur. As a child she felt drawn to give her life to God and, after some resistance from her family, joined the Carmelite sisters of the Syro-Malabar Church (today the Congregation of the Mother of Carmel), taking the name Euphrasia of the Sacred Heart of Jesus.

She suffered serious illnesses as a young sister and attributed her recovery to the intercession of the Holy Family. For many years she lived at St Mary's Convent, Ollur, where she served as novice mistress and superior. She spent long hours before the Blessed Sacrament, and people came to her for prayer and counsel.

The people of Ollur called her the “praying mother” (Prarthikkunna Amma), and also the “moving tabernacle”, because Christ seemed to go with her wherever she went. She died on 29 August 1952. She was beatified in 2006 and canonised by Pope Francis on 23 November 2014, together with St Kuriakose Elias Chavara.
lessons: Prayer is a work
Euphrasia's main apostolate was prayer. Her intercession sustained many families.
Close to the tabernacle
Her love for the Eucharist made her a “moving tabernacle” for others.
Faithful in ordinary duties
As novice mistress and superior she guided others with gentleness and firmness.
Hidden holiness
She did not seek attention; people simply knew that she prayed for them.
stories: People of every background came to the convent at Ollur asking “Amma” to pray for their needs: sick children, debts, exams, family quarrels. She would promise to pray, and she kept her promise, often late into the night in the chapel.
euphrasia.prayer: Lord Jesus, you gave St Euphrasia a heart burning with love for your Sacred Heart and a life of constant prayer. Through her intercession teach us to pray always and not lose heart, and to carry you to others. Amen.

points: Rosa Eluvathingal desired to give her life to God.
Her recovery from illness, attributed to the Holy Family.
Long hours before the Blessed Sacrament at Ollur.
Novice mistress and superior, simple and kind.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the people of Ollur called St Euphrasia the praying mother. She did not do spectacular things. She prayed, and she did her daily duties faithfully, with great love. That was her holiness.

Rosa Eluvathingal was born at Kattoor in 1877. As a child she felt God calling her, and despite resistance from her family she joined the Carmelite sisters, taking the name Euphrasia of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. As a young sister she suffered serious illness and attributed her recovery to the intercession of the Holy Family.

For many years she lived at St Mary's Convent, Ollur, as novice mistress and superior. She spent long hours before the Blessed Sacrament. People came to her with their troubles, and she listened and prayed. She was faithful in small duties: sweeping, teaching, correcting, encouraging.

Euphrasia reminds us that prayer is real work. A world that values only activity needs people who pray. Let us visit the Blessed Sacrament this week, even for five minutes, and bring to the Lord the troubles of our families. And let us ask St Euphrasia to pray for us.

opts.a: In the light of the Word: pray always and do not lose heart
points: Pray always and not lose heart (Luke 18:1–8).
Your Father who sees in secret (Matthew 6:6).
Abide in me as I abide in you (John 15:4–5).
homily: Dear friends, Jesus told a parable about a widow who kept asking an unjust judge for justice until he gave in. He told it so that His disciples would pray always and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). St Euphrasia lived this parable.

Prayer is not always easy. Sometimes we pray and nothing seems to change. Euphrasia also knew illness and difficulty. But she kept praying, day after day, before the tabernacle. Jesus said: when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret (Matthew 6:6). Her holiness was mostly hidden.

Jesus also said: abide in me as I abide in you; apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:4–5). Euphrasia's long hours before the Blessed Sacrament were not wasted time. From that union came her wisdom, her kindness and her strength.

Martha served; Mary sat at the Lord's feet and listened, and Jesus said she had chosen the better part (Luke 10:42). We need both. But in our busy lives, let us not lose Mary's part. Give God a fixed time every day. Do not lose heart.

opts.a: For young people and families: the power of a praying mother
points: Many of us are believers because someone prayed for us.
Pray for your children by name
Do not give up on a wandering child.
homily: Dear families, St Euphrasia was called the praying mother, though she never had children of her own. In a sense she became a mother to everyone who came to her for prayer. Many of us here are believers today because a mother or grandmother prayed for us.

Parents, pray for your children by name every day. Pray for their studies, their friends, their future spouse, their faith. Pray especially when they wander or struggle. St Monica prayed for years for her son Augustine. Do not give up.

Teach your children to visit Jesus in the church, even for five minutes, after school or on the way home. Euphrasia spent hours before the tabernacle; children can start with a few minutes. They will remember it all their lives.
Young people, you too can pray for your parents, your friends and your future. Prayer is not only for the old. Ask St Euphrasia to teach you to pray with trust, and never to lose heart.

mariamthresia.t: Founder of the Congregation of the Holy Family, apostle of families
word: And the king will answer them, “Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me.”
Matthew 25:40
life: Thresia was born on 26 April 1876 at Puthenchira, Thrissur district. Her family had once been wealthy but became poor. As a young woman she gave herself to prayer and penance and, with a few companions, began to visit homes, care for the sick, nurse those with infectious diseases whom others avoided, and help families in crisis.

She experienced intense mystical graces and also long periods of spiritual trial. Her spiritual director, Fr Joseph Vithayathil, guided her carefully. In 1914, with the approval of the bishop of Thrissur, she founded the Congregation of the Holy Family (CHF), dedicated to the care of families, the education of girls and service of the poor.
She died on 8 June 1926 at Kuzhikattussery. She was beatified by Pope St John Paul II in 2000 and canonised by Pope Francis on 13 October 2019, together with St John Henry Newman.
lessons: The family is a mission field
Mariam Thresia went into homes, brought peace to quarrelling families and prayed with them.
Serve those whom others avoid
She nursed the sick and the dying, even those with contagious diseases.
Obedience to spiritual guidance
She submitted her extraordinary experiences to the Church's discernment.
The Holy Family as model
She named her congregation after the Holy Family because every home should resemble Nazareth.
stories: With her companions, Thresia went to houses where there was illness, poverty or conflict. She cleaned, cooked, nursed, prayed with the family and urged reconciliation. Many families were reunited through her patient presence.
mariamthresia.prayer: Lord God, you gave St Mariam Thresia a great love for families and for the poor. Through her prayers bless our homes with peace, heal broken families, and make us servants of the sick and the lonely. Amen.

points: A once-wealthy family became poor; she learned compassion.
Nursing the sick, even with infectious diseases.
Founder of the Congregation of the Holy Family (1914).
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, St Mariam Thresia of Puthenchira is called the apostle of families. In her time, many families were broken by poverty, illness, alcohol and quarrels. She went into those homes with prayer and practical love.

Thresia was born in 1876 into a family that had once been rich but had become poor. She knew hardship. With a few companions she began to visit homes, to nurse the sick, even those with infectious diseases whom others avoided, and to help families in crisis. Jesus said: just as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40).

She received great spiritual graces and also went through long periods of trial. Through all of it she obeyed her spiritual director, Fr Joseph Vithayathil, and her bishop. In 1914 she founded the Congregation of the Holy Family to serve families, educate girls and care for the poor.

Today families face new storms: migration, debt, addiction, screens, broken marriages. Mariam Thresia teaches us to go to those families with prayer and help, not with gossip and judgement. Let us pray for struggling families in our parish, and ask her intercession for our own homes.

opts.a: In the light of the Word: you did it to me
points: We will be judged on how we treated the least (Matthew 25:31–46).
I was sick and you visited me.
Mariam Thresia nursed those with contagious disease.
homily: Dear friends, the word for St Mariam Thresia is from the judgement scene in Matthew: just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40). On the last day, Christ will not ask about our titles or wealth, but about the hungry, the sick and the stranger.

Jesus hides Himself in the poor and suffering. I was sick and you visited me. Mariam Thresia took these words literally. She went to homes where others would not go, nursed the dying, washed the sick, and comforted families in despair.

When a leper came to Jesus, Jesus stretched out His hand and touched him (Mark 1:41). Lepers were untouchable, but Jesus touched. Mariam Thresia nursed people with contagious diseases when others kept their distance. Love is not afraid to touch the wounded.

Who are the least in our parish today? The sick person alone at home, the family drowning in debt, the alcoholic and his wife and children, the migrant worker far from home. Let us not pass by. When we serve them, we serve Christ.

opts.a: For young people and families: building a holy family
points: Prayer, work and love in Nazareth.
Alcohol and drugs destroy homes; seek help early.
Children can bring peace at home.
homily: Dear families, St Mariam Thresia gave her congregation the name of the Holy Family, because she believed every family can learn from Nazareth: Jesus, Mary and Joseph prayed together, worked hard, and loved one another.

Every family has wounds: quarrels, harsh words, money problems, old resentments. Mariam Thresia visited such homes and brought peace through prayer, patience and practical help. In your home, start with small things: speak kindly, apologise quickly, pray together every evening.

One great enemy of families today is addiction: alcohol, drugs, gambling, even the phone. If someone in your family is struggling, do not hide it in shame. Seek help early: from the parish, a counsellor, a de-addiction centre. Love sometimes means firm action.

Young people, you can be peacemakers at home. When your parents are tired or tense, help without being asked, avoid adding to the conflict, and pray for them. Ask St Mariam Thresia to make your home a holy family.

devasahayam.t: Layman and martyr, first lay saint of India
word: Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven.
Matthew 10:32
life: Neelakanta Pillai was born on 23 April 1712 at Nattalam, in present-day Kanyakumari district, then part of the kingdom of Travancore. He served as an official in the administration of Maharaja Marthanda Varma, the able ruler who built and unified Travancore.

Through his friendship with Eustachius De Lannoy, a Dutch naval officer who had entered the service of Travancore after the battle of Colachel (1741), he came to know Christ. He was baptised in 1745 by the Jesuit missionary Fr Giovanni Battista Buttari at Vadakkankulam, taking the name Lazarus, in Tamil and Malayalam Devasahayam, “God is my help”.

In a society where public office, caste and religious duties were closely bound together, his conversion and his refusal to give up his faith led to his arrest in 1749. After a long imprisonment and much suffering, he was shot dead on 14 January 1752 at Aralvaimozhy. His remains rest in St Francis Xavier Cathedral, Kottar. He was beatified at Nagercoil in 2012 and canonised by Pope Francis on 15 May 2022, the first Indian layman to be declared a saint.
lessons: Faith is worth everything
Devasahayam gave up position and security rather than deny Christ.
Friendship can lead to God
The witness of a foreign friend opened the way to his faith.
Equality in Christ
As a Christian he treated people of every caste as brothers and sisters, which was costly in his time.
Forgiveness and patience
Tradition remembers him praying and bearing his sufferings without bitterness.
stories: The place of his martyrdom near Aralvaimozhy, Kattadimalai, has become a place of pilgrimage. Tradition says that he knelt in prayer before he was shot.
devasahayam.prayer: Lord God, you strengthened St Devasahayam to confess Christ even unto death. Through his prayers give us courage to live our faith openly, respect for every person, and peace among all communities of our land. Amen.

points: Neelakanta Pillai, a trusted official in Travancore, met Christ through his friend Eustachius De Lannoy.
God is my help: baptised in 1745.
He would not give up Christ, accepting imprisonment and suffering.
Martyr and first lay saint of India
Died at Aralvaimozhi in 1752; canonised in 2022.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, St Devasahayam was a layman, a husband and an official, not a priest or religious. He is the first lay saint of India, and his life shows what it means to put Christ above everything.

Neelakanta Pillai served in the administration of Maharaja Marthanda Varma, the able ruler who built and unified Travancore. Through his friendship with Eustachius De Lannoy, a Dutch officer in the king's service, he came to know Christ, and in 1745 he was baptised with the name Lazarus, Devasahayam, God is my help. Friendship led him to faith.

In that society, public office, caste and religious duties were closely bound together, and his conversion and his treatment of all people as equal created serious conflict with the established order. He was arrested and suffered imprisonment and hardship for several years. He did not give up his faith, and he prayed for those who made him suffer. In 1752 he was shot to death at Aralvaimozhi.

Devasahayam teaches us that faith is worth everything, that Christ makes all people equal, and that we should answer suffering with prayer and forgiveness, not with hatred. Let us ask his intercession for all who suffer for their faith, and for the courage to acknowledge Christ before others (Matthew 10:32).

opts.a: In the light of the Word: acknowledging Christ before others
points: Everyone who acknowledges me before others (Matthew 10:32).
Faith can bring division even in families (Matthew 10:34–36).
Pray for those who persecute you (Matthew 5:44).
homily: Dear friends, Jesus said: everyone who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven (Matthew 10:32). St Devasahayam acknowledged Christ publicly, at the cost of his position, his comfort and finally his life.

In the same chapter Jesus warned that faith in Him could bring division, even within families (Matthew 10:34–36). This was true for Devasahayam. His decision to follow Christ brought him into conflict with the social and religious order of his time and with people close to him. Following Christ is not always comfortable.

Jesus also said: those who lose their life for my sake will find it (Matthew 10:39). By the world's measure, Devasahayam lost everything. By God's measure, he found eternal life, and today the whole Church honours him.

But notice how he suffered: without hatred. The accounts of his martyrdom say that he prayed for those who caused his suffering. Jesus said: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matthew 5:44). Let us honour him by acknowledging Christ boldly and by forgiving those who hurt us.

opts.a: For young people and families: friendship, equality and courage
points: A friend who leads to God
De Lannoy's friendship brought him to Christ.
Devasahayam treated people of every caste as brothers and sisters.
Holiness in ordinary jobs and marriage.
Firm in faith, respectful to all.
homily: Dear young people and families, St Devasahayam came to Christ through a friend. Eustachius De Lannoy shared his faith with him, and that friendship changed his life. Ask yourself: do my friends lead me closer to God or further away? And am I a friend who leads others to God?

After his baptism Devasahayam treated people of every caste as equals, brothers and sisters in Christ. That was revolutionary in his time, and it is still challenging today. In Christ there is no higher or lower person. Let us root out every form of caste prejudice and discrimination from our hearts and our communities.
Devasahayam was a layman, a husband, an official. He shows that holiness is not only for priests and sisters. You can be a saint as a student, an engineer, a nurse, a government officer, a parent.

He was firm in faith, yet he did not hate. He respected the authority of his land and prayed for those who caused his suffering. Be like him: firm in your faith, respectful to people of every religion, and courageous when you must stand for what is right.

francisxavier.t: Jesuit priest, Apostle of the Indies, patron of the missions
word: And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.”
Mark 16:15
life: Francis Xavier was born in 1506 at the castle of Javier in Navarre, Spain. As a student in Paris he shared a room with Ignatius of Loyola, who repeated to him the words of Jesus: “What will it profit them if they gain the whole world but forfeit their life?” (Matthew 16:26) Francis became one of the first companions of Ignatius and a founding member of the Society of Jesus.

Sent to the East at the request of the King of Portugal, he arrived in Goa on 6 May 1542. He worked among the pearl fishers of the Fishery Coast, along the coast of Travancore, then in Malacca, the Moluccas and Japan. He taught the catechism in simple songs, cared for the sick in hospitals and baptised many thousands.

He died on 3 December 1552 on the island of Shangchuan, within sight of the coast of China, which he longed to enter. His body is venerated in the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Goa. He was canonised in 1622 together with St Ignatius, and in 1927 was named, with St Thérèse of Lisieux, patron of the missions.
lessons: What does it profit?
One question from a friend changed Francis's ambitions from worldly success to the Kingdom of God.
Mission needs zeal
He travelled thousands of miles by sea and on foot, in hardship, to bring Christ to others.
Teach simply
He put the prayers and catechism into simple verses that children and fishermen could sing.
Obedience and friendship
His letters show deep love and obedience towards Ignatius and his brothers.
stories: In a letter of 1544 he wrote that many people were not becoming Christians only because there was no one to teach them, and that he often thought of going round the universities of Europe crying out like a madman to awaken students to this need.
A popular legend says that during a storm Francis held his crucifix in the waves and lost it, and that a crab brought it back to him on the shore.
quotes: Many, many people hereabouts are not becoming Christians for one reason only: there is nobody to make them Christians.
St Francis Xavier, letter to St Ignatius and companions (1544), Office of Readings, 3 December
francisxavier.prayer: Lord God, through the preaching of St Francis Xavier you brought many peoples of the East to the faith. Give us his zeal for the Gospel, so that the Church may rejoice in new sons and daughters everywhere. Amen.

points: A question that changed a life
What will it profit them to gain the whole world? (Matthew 16:26).
Goa 1542, the Fishery Coast, Travancore, Malacca, Japan.
Catechism in songs, care for the sick.
Dying with his eyes on China
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, St Francis Xavier was a brilliant young man at the University of Paris, ambitious for a fine career. His roommate, Ignatius of Loyola, kept repeating to him the words of Jesus: what will it profit them if they gain the whole world but forfeit their life? (Matthew 16:26). Slowly the question entered Francis's heart, and it changed his life.

He became one of the first Jesuits and was sent to the East. He arrived in Goa in 1542 and worked among the pearl fishers of the Fishery Coast and along the coast of Travancore, then in Malacca, the Moluccas and Japan. He taught the catechism in simple songs that children could sing, cared for the sick in hospitals and baptised many thousands.

His letters to Europe burn with zeal. He wrote that he felt like going through the universities shouting like a madman, to tell students that many people were not becoming Christians because there was no one to teach them. He died in 1552 on the island of Sancian, within sight of China, which he longed to enter. His body is venerated in Goa.

Francis Xavier asks us the same question Ignatius asked him: what does it profit? What are we living for? Let us pray for missionaries, support the missions, and share our faith with joy where we live.

opts.a: In the light of the Word: go into all the world
points: Go into all the world and proclaim the good news (Mark 16:15).
Pray the Lord of the harvest (Matthew 9:37–38).
homily: Dear friends, the word chosen for St Francis Xavier is the command of the risen Lord: go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation (Mark 16:15). Francis took it literally. He travelled thousands of miles by sea, in dangerous conditions, to bring the Gospel to people who had never heard it.

St Paul asks: how are they to believe in one of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone to proclaim Him? (Romans 10:14). Francis was moved by this question. He saw children who were baptised but untaught, villages without priests, people eager to learn. So he taught, and trained catechists.

Jesus said: the harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers (Matthew 9:37–38). Francis begged Europe to send more missionaries. Today the harvest is still plentiful, in India and around the world. Let us pray for vocations and support missionaries.

Francis could do all this because he trusted the promise: I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). Mission is not our project; it is Christ's work through us. Wherever you live, you too are sent. Proclaim the good news by word and life.

opts.a: For young people and families: ambition and generosity
points: Francis was ambitious; Christ redirected his ambition.
Ignatius did not give up on him.
Teach the faith to your own children first.
homily: Dear young people, St Francis Xavier was ambitious. He wanted to be a great professor, admired and successful. Ambition is not bad; God gave you gifts to use. But Francis discovered that the greatest ambition is to give your life to God and others.

His roommate Ignatius did not give up on him. For years he kept asking: what does it profit to gain the whole world and lose your soul? Friends who challenge us to be better are a gift. Choose such friends, and be such a friend.
Whatever your studies or career, ask: how can I use this for God and for people? A doctor, engineer, teacher or businessperson can be a missionary in their field, by honesty, generosity and witness.

Parents, Francis taught the faith to children in simple songs. You are the first missionaries to your children. Teach them prayers, Bible stories and songs. Some of them may hear God's call to the priesthood, religious life or mission. Do not stand in their way; it would be the greatest honour for your family.

joseph.n: St Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary
joseph.t: Guardian of the Redeemer, Patron of the Universal Church
word: When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him; he took her as his wife,
Matthew 1:24
life: Joseph, a descendant of King David, lived in Nazareth as a carpenter (Matthew 13:55). He was betrothed to Mary. When he learned that she was with child, being “a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace”, he planned to dismiss her quietly; but an angel told him in a dream that the child was from the Holy Spirit. Joseph obeyed and took Mary into his home.

He gave Jesus his name and, as his legal father, placed him in the line of David. He protected the Child and his mother on the journey to Bethlehem, in the flight to Egypt and on the return to Nazareth. He taught Jesus to work, to pray and to keep the Law. The Gospels record not a single word of his; they record his actions.

He probably died before the public ministry of Jesus, and Christian tradition honours him as patron of a happy death, dying in the arms of Jesus and Mary. Blessed Pius IX declared him Patron of the Universal Church in 1870. Pope St John Paul II wrote Redemptoris Custos (1989) and Pope Francis Patris Corde (2020) about him.
lessons: Silent and faithful
Joseph speaks through obedience. Holiness does not need many words.
Just and merciful
He would not expose Mary to disgrace: justice with mercy.
The dignity of work
The Son of God learnt a trade from Joseph; ordinary work can be holy.
A father who protects
Joseph rose at night and acted at once to protect his family. Fathers today are called to the same courage.
stories: An angel warned Joseph in a dream that Herod wanted to kill the child. That very night he took Mary and Jesus and fled to Egypt (Matthew 2:13–15).
St Teresa of Ávila had great devotion to St Joseph and spread it among her Carmelite sisters; she wrote that she could not remember asking him for anything that he had failed to obtain.
quotes: I do not remember even now that I have ever asked anything of him which he has failed to grant.
St Teresa of Ávila, The Book of Her Life, chapter 6
joseph.prayer: Almighty God, you entrusted the beginnings of our salvation to the faithful care of St Joseph. Through his intercession may your Church protect the mystery of salvation, and may our fathers and families imitate his faith, obedience and love. Amen.

points: Faithful to God's law, merciful to Mary (Matthew 1:19).
He did as the angel commanded
Protector of the Child and His mother
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, St Joseph never speaks a word in the Gospels, but his actions speak loudly. He is called a righteous man (Matthew 1:19): faithful to God's law, yet merciful. When he discovered Mary was with child, he did not want to expose her to shame.

When the angel told him in a dream that the child was from the Holy Spirit, Joseph woke and did as the angel commanded (Matthew 1:24). He took Mary into his home, gave Jesus His name, and as legal father placed Him in the line of David. His obedience was prompt and complete.

Joseph protected Jesus and Mary through every danger: the journey to Bethlehem, the flight to Egypt, the return to Nazareth. He worked as a carpenter to support them and taught Jesus to work, to pray and to keep the Law. Pope Pius IX declared him Patron of the Universal Church: he who guarded the Holy Family now guards the Church.
Fathers, workers, and all who protect others, look to St Joseph. Go to Joseph with your needs, as St Teresa of Ávila advised. And let us ask him to guard our families and our Church.

opts.a: In the light of the Word: the dreams of Joseph
points: Joseph of Egypt and Joseph of Nazareth
Two dreamers who saved their families (Genesis 37; 41).
homily: Dear friends, the Bible has two famous Josephs, and both were dreamers. Joseph, son of Jacob, dreamed dreams, was sold into Egypt and became the saviour of his family in a time of famine; he told Pharaoh: go to Joseph (Genesis 41:55). Joseph of Nazareth also received God's guidance in dreams and also went down to Egypt to save his family.

Four times in the first chapters of Matthew an angel speaks to Joseph in a dream: take Mary as your wife; flee to Egypt; return to Israel; go to Galilee. Each time the message comes in the night, when Joseph is helpless. God often speaks to us in the dark moments of life, when our own plans fail.
Joseph did not understand everything. He was not told how the story would end. He had to trust. Faith is not having all the answers; it is obeying God step by step.
And each time, Joseph rose and did what he was told. He did not argue or delay. Many of us know God's will but postpone it. Let us learn from Joseph to wake up to God's will and do it today.

opts.a: For young people and families: a father's love
points: Guarding the family's body and soul.
Earning a living without losing the family.
Young men: preparing to be fathers
homily: Dear families, St Joseph is the model for fathers. He protected Mary and Jesus from danger, worked hard to support them and taught Jesus the faith. A father's first task is to protect his family, not only from physical danger but also from what harms the soul.
Joseph's strength was tender. He did not want to shame Mary. Fathers, be strong without being harsh. Correct your children without humiliating them. Show affection. Let your children see you pray.

Many fathers today work far from home, in the Gulf or abroad. Joseph also lived in exile for his family's sake. Even at a distance, stay present: call, listen, pray for your family daily, and do not let money become more important than love.

Young men, you are preparing to be husbands and fathers. Learn from Joseph: purity, responsibility, hard work and faith. A real man is not one who dominates, but one who protects and serves. Go to Joseph and ask him to make you such a man.

antony.t: Franciscan priest, Doctor of the Church
word: proclaim the message; be persistent whether the time is favorable or unfavorable; convince, rebuke, and encourage, with the utmost patience in teaching.
2 Timothy 4:2
life: Fernando Martins was born in Lisbon, Portugal, around 1195. He became an Augustinian canon and studied the Scriptures deeply. When the bodies of five Franciscan friars martyred in Morocco were brought to Coimbra in 1220, he was so moved that he joined the Franciscans, taking the name Antony, and set out for Africa to preach.

Illness forced him to return, and a storm drove his ship to Sicily. He lived hidden in a small hermitage in Italy until, at an ordination at Forlì, he was asked to preach without preparation; his learning and fire astonished everyone. St Francis himself entrusted him with teaching theology to the friars. He preached in Italy and France to great crowds, calling sinners to conversion and defending the poor against usurers.

He died near Padua on 13 June 1231, about 36 years old. He was canonised in 1232, less than a year after his death, and Pope Pius XII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1946. Throughout the world, and in countless Kerala homes and churches, people pray to him on Tuesdays and ask his help.
lessons: Preach with your life
Antony taught that actions speak louder than words.
Love the Word of God
His preaching was full of Scripture, which he knew almost by heart.
Hidden years prepare great work
Before his preaching became famous he served quietly and humbly.
Charity to the poor
The custom of “St Antony's bread”, alms for the hungry in his honour, keeps his love for the poor alive.
stories: When the people of Rimini refused to listen, Antony went to the shore and began to preach to the fish, and they gathered to listen; the townspeople were moved to repentance. The story comes from the Little Flowers of St Francis.

A novice ran away with Antony's psalter, which contained his notes. Antony prayed, and the novice returned the book and came back to the community. This is the origin of the custom of asking St Antony to help find lost things.
quotes: Actions speak louder than words; let your words teach and your actions speak.
St Antony of Padua, Sermons, Office of Readings, 13 June
antony.prayer: Almighty God, you gave St Antony to your people as an outstanding preacher and a helper in their needs. Through his intercession help us to follow the Gospel, to love the poor, and to find again whatever we have lost, above all your grace. Amen.

points: Moved by the martyrs of Morocco, he became a friar (1220).
Unknown in a small hermitage until called to preach.
Learned and fiery, calling sinners to conversion.
Charity to the poor; St Antony's bread.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, St Antony is loved all over the world, and many pray to him to find lost things. But he was first of all a great preacher of the Word of God and a friend of the poor.

Fernando Martins was born in Lisbon around 1195 and became an Augustinian canon, studying the Scriptures deeply. When the bodies of five Franciscans martyred in Morocco were brought to Coimbra, he was so moved that he joined the Franciscans, taking the name Antony, and set out for Africa. Illness forced him back, and a storm took his ship to Italy.

For a while he lived unknown in a small hermitage. Then, at an ordination, he was asked to preach without preparation, and everyone was astonished at his learning and fire. St Francis entrusted him with teaching theology to the friars. He preached to great crowds, calling sinners to repentance and defending the poor. He died in 1231, aged about thirty-six, and is a Doctor of the Church.

Antony said: let your words teach and your actions speak. Let us honour him by loving the Word of God, by our charity to the poor, and by asking his help to find not only lost things, but lost faith and lost people.

opts.a: In the light of the Word: preach the word in season and out
points: Be persistent whether the time is favourable or unfavourable (2 Timothy 4:2).
Antony challenged injustice and comforted sinners.
homily: Dear friends, St Paul told Timothy: proclaim the message; be persistent whether the time is favourable or unfavourable; convince, rebuke and encourage, with the utmost patience in teaching (2 Timothy 4:2). St Antony lived this charge.

Antony knew the Scriptures so well that Pope Gregory IX called him the ark of the testament. The Word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword (Hebrews 4:12). When Antony preached, hearts were cut to the core and people went to confession in great numbers.
He did not only comfort; he also rebuked. He preached against greed and usury that crushed the poor. He was courageous before the powerful. Yet he always encouraged sinners to hope in God's mercy.

Not all of us are preachers, but all of us are called to share the Word. Read the Bible daily. Let it convince, rebuke and encourage you first. Then share it with patience, in your family and among friends.

opts.a: For young people and families: finding what is lost
points: Lost things and the lost son
homily: Dear young people and families, many of us pray to St Antony when we lose keys, phones or documents. That is a sign of trust, and it is good. But let us ask: what more important things have we lost?

Some have lost the habit of prayer, or Sunday {Q}. Some have lost peace in the family, or a friendship through a quarrel. Some have lost hope. Jesus told of a shepherd looking for a lost sheep, a woman searching for a lost coin and a father waiting for a lost son (Luke 15). God searches for what is lost. Ask St Antony to help you find what matters most.

In many places, when people receive a favour through St Antony, they give bread or money for the poor. This custom is beautiful: our thanksgiving becomes charity. When God helps you, help someone else.
Young people, Antony loved study, especially the Scriptures. Study well, and learn your faith deeply. A faith that is understood is stronger in times of temptation and doubt.

word: Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life.
Revelation 2:10
life: Sebastian was a Christian martyr in Rome, probably during the persecution of the emperor Diocletian at the end of the 3rd century. St Ambrose of Milan, writing in the 4th century, mentions him as a native of Milan who suffered in Rome. He was buried on the Via Appia, where the Basilica of St Sebastian and its catacomb stand today.

A later account of his martyrdom (5th century) tells that he was an officer in the imperial guard who secretly encouraged Christians in prison. When his faith was discovered he was tied to a post and shot with arrows, left for dead, nursed back to health by a Christian widow named Irene, and then, after boldly confronting the emperor, beaten to death. Historians regard many details of this account as legendary, but his martyrdom and early veneration are certain.

Sebastian became one of the most loved saints of the Church, invoked especially in times of plague and epidemic. In Kerala countless churches are dedicated to him, and his feast in January, with processions of the arrows (ambu perunnal), is among the great festivals of many parishes.
lessons: Courage in hidden places
According to tradition he used his position to strengthen others in their faith.
Faithful until death
He did not give up Christ even after surviving the first attempt on his life.
Faith in times of epidemic
Christians have turned to his intercession in plagues; we too may ask his help for the sick.
A soldier of Christ
Every Christian is called to the courage of a soldier, without hatred.
stories: The best-known image of Sebastian shows him tied to a tree, pierced with arrows. It comes from the account of his first martyrdom, which he survived.
The tradition says that Irene, widow of a martyr, came at night to bury him and found him still alive, and nursed him back to health.
sebastian.prayer: Lord God, you gave St Sebastian the strength to remain faithful until death. Through his intercession protect us from epidemic and disease, give strength to the sick, and make us courageous witnesses of Christ. Amen.

points: Probably under Diocletian, late 3rd century; mentioned by St Ambrose.
According to a later account, an officer who strengthened imprisoned Christians.
The tradition of his first martyrdom by arrows.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, St Sebastian is one of the most popular saints in Kerala; many parishes celebrate his feast with great devotion. What do we know about him?

History tells us that Sebastian was a Christian martyr in Rome, probably during the persecution of Diocletian at the end of the third century. St Ambrose, writing in the fourth century, mentions him. He was buried on the Via Appia, where his basilica stands today.

A later account of his martyrdom, from the fifth century, tells that he was an officer in the imperial guard who secretly encouraged Christians in prison. When his faith was discovered, he was tied to a post and shot with arrows, left for dead, nursed by a Christian widow, and later beaten to death after confronting the emperor. These details belong to tradition, and some are legendary; but the heart of the story is certain: Sebastian gave his life rather than deny Christ.

The risen Lord says: be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life (Revelation 2:10). Let us honour St Sebastian not only with processions and fireworks, but with courage and fidelity in our faith.

opts.a: In the light of the Word: the crown of life
points: Do not fear what you are about to suffer
homily: Dear friends, the risen Christ says to the Church in Smyrna: do not fear what you are about to suffer; be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life (Revelation 2:10). These words fit St Sebastian perfectly.

Tradition remembers Sebastian as a soldier. St Paul uses a soldier's image: put on the whole armour of God, the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:13–17). Sebastian's true armour was not Roman steel, but faith.

The tradition says he used his position to encourage Christians in prison. Paul writes: encourage one another and build up each other (1 Thessalonians 5:11). Whatever our position, we can use it to strengthen those who are weak in faith.

At the end of his life Paul said: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; there is reserved for me the crown of righteousness (2 Timothy 4:7–8). Let us ask St Sebastian to help us keep the faith until the end.

opts.a: For young people and families: true devotion at the feast
points: A saint in times of epidemic
Christians invoked him in plagues; we pray and also care.
No alcohol abuse or wasteful show; share with the poor.
homily: Dear young people and families, the feast of St Sebastian is a big celebration in many parishes, with processions, arrows, music and fireworks. Celebrations are good. But let us ask: does our feast lead us closer to Christ, as Sebastian was?

For centuries Christians prayed to St Sebastian in times of plague. Faith and responsibility go together: we pray for protection, and we also care for the sick, follow good health practice and help the poor in times of epidemic.

Sebastian, according to tradition, kept his faith in the emperor's guard, a place where Christians were in danger. Young people, at school, college and work you may be the only person who prays or goes to church. Do not hide it. Be respectful, but be brave.
Let our feasts be holy: no excessive drinking, no wasteful display, no quarrels. Let part of the feast money go to the poor. Then St Sebastian, who gave everything for Christ, will be truly honoured.

word: Put on the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
Ephesians 6:11
life: George was a Christian martyr who died at Lydda (today Lod, in Israel), probably in the persecution of Diocletian around the year 303. Veneration of him spread very early throughout East and West; churches were built over his tomb at Lydda, and he is honoured in the Eastern Churches as a “Great Martyr”.

Ancient accounts say that he was a soldier who refused to deny Christ and was tortured and beheaded. Pope Gelasius I (494) already remarked that his deeds were known to God, while many stories about him were uncertain. The famous story of George slaying a dragon to save a princess appears only in the Middle Ages, especially in the Golden Legend (13th century), and is a legend that pictures the victory of faith over evil.
In Kerala George (Geevarghese) is one of the most loved saints. Great pilgrim churches such as Edathua and Aruvithura are dedicated to him, and his feast in April and May draws huge crowds.
lessons: Faith over fear
George chose Christ over his career and his life.
Fight evil with God's armour
The dragon is a picture of sin and evil; we overcome it with faith, prayer, truth and the Word of God.
A soldier who serves
Strength is given to protect the weak, as the legend shows him rescuing the helpless.
A saint for East and West
George is honoured by Christians of every tradition, a sign of the one faith.
stories: The legend tells of a dragon that terrorised a city and demanded human victims. George, passing by, made the sign of the cross, overcame the dragon, and the people of the city were baptised. It is a medieval legend, a picture of Christ's victory over evil.
george.prayer: Lord God, you gave St George the courage to confess Christ to the end. Through his intercession clothe us with the armour of faith, protect us from every evil, and make us strong defenders of the weak. Amen.

points: A Great Martyr in the Eastern Churches.
A medieval story (Golden Legend) picturing the victory of faith over evil.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, St George is honoured all over the world, in East and West. In Kerala many churches are dedicated to him, and his image with the dragon is very familiar. What do we really know?

George was a Christian martyr who died at Lydda, in the Holy Land, probably in the persecution of Diocletian around the year 303. Veneration of him spread very early; churches were built over his tomb, and the Eastern Churches call him a Great Martyr. Ancient accounts say he was a soldier who refused to deny Christ and was tortured and beheaded. Already in the fifth century Pope Gelasius said that his deeds were known to God, while many stories about him were uncertain.

The famous story of George killing a dragon to rescue a princess appears only in the Middle Ages and is a legend. But legends can teach truth. The dragon is a picture of evil; the knight is a picture of faith that defeats evil with God's help.

Let us honour St George by fighting the real dragons in our lives and society: sin, addiction, injustice, fear. And let us put on the whole armour of God (Ephesians 6:11), trusting that Christ has already won the victory.

opts.a: In the light of the Word: the armour of God
points: The belt of truth and breastplate of righteousness
Quenching the flaming arrows of the evil one (Ephesians 6:16).
The Word of God and prayer (Ephesians 6:17–18).
homily: Dear friends, the word chosen for St George is: put on the whole armour of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil (Ephesians 6:11). George was a soldier, and he knew that the real battle is spiritual.

Paul says our struggle is not against enemies of flesh and blood, but against spiritual forces of evil (Ephesians 6:12). Our enemies are not other people, but sin and the evil one who tempts us. That is why Christians do not hate.

The armour is described piece by piece: the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, shoes ready to proclaim the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God (Ephesians 6:14–17). Truth, integrity, faith and the Scriptures are our weapons.

And Paul adds: pray in the Spirit at all times (Ephesians 6:18). George was victorious because he stood firm in faith and prayer. Let us dress each morning in this armour with a short prayer, and face our dragons without fear.

opts.a: For young people and families: fighting today's dragons
points: The princess in the story: defend those in danger.
homily: Dear young people, everyone loves the picture of St George on his horse defeating the dragon. It is a legend from the Middle Ages, not history, but it carries a true message: with God's help, evil can be defeated.

What is your dragon? Maybe pornography, drugs, alcohol, gaming addiction, anger, lying or laziness. Name it honestly. Then fight it with the weapons of God: prayer, confession, the Eucharist, good friends, and if needed, professional help.

Christian courage is not violence. George did not fight people for his faith; he suffered for it. Be brave, but never aggressive. And like the knight in the story, protect the weak: the bullied classmate, the girl who is harassed, the child who is in danger.

Families, teach your children to love the saints truthfully: what is history, what is tradition, what is legend. The truth of the faith does not need exaggeration. St George's real glory is that he chose Christ over his life.

teresakolkata.t: Founder of the Missionaries of Charity
word: After this, when Jesus knew that all was now finished, he said (in order to fulfill the scripture), “I am thirsty.”
John 19:28
life: Agnes Gonxha Bojaxhiu was born on 26 August 1910 in Skopje. At eighteen she joined the Sisters of Loreto and came to India in 1929, where she taught for many years at St Mary's School in Kolkata.

On 10 September 1946, on a train to Darjeeling, she received what she called a “call within the call”: to serve Christ in the poorest of the poor. In 1948 she began work in the slums, and in 1950 founded the Missionaries of Charity. She opened a home for the dying at Kalighat, homes for abandoned children, lepers and the sick, and her sisters spread throughout the world. In every chapel of her congregation the words of Jesus on the Cross are written beside the crucifix: “I thirst.”

She received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979. After her death it became known that for many years she had lived in deep interior darkness, without feeling God's presence, yet faithful in prayer and service. She died in Kolkata on 5 September 1997, was beatified in 2003 and canonised by Pope Francis on 4 September 2016.
lessons: Jesus thirsts for love
Behind all her work was Jesus' cry “I thirst”: thirst for souls and for love.
Small things with great love
She taught that what matters is not the size of the work but the love put into it.
See Christ in the poor
She served Jesus “in the distressing disguise of the poorest of the poor”.
Faithful in darkness
Even without consolation she kept praying and loving; faith is more than feelings.
stories: In her early days she found a dying woman on a Kolkata street, partly eaten by rats and ants, whom a hospital would not take. She stayed with her until she died. Out of such encounters grew the home for the dying at Kalighat, Nirmal Hriday.
Receiving the Nobel Prize, she asked that the money for the banquet be given to the poor, and spoke of the poverty of loneliness in rich countries, urging families to love one another first at home.
quotes: The fruit of silence is prayer. The fruit of prayer is faith. The fruit of faith is love. The fruit of love is service. The fruit of service is peace.
St Teresa of Calcutta
We ourselves feel that what we are doing is just a drop in the ocean. But the ocean would be less because of that missing drop.
St Teresa of Calcutta
teresakolkata.prayer: Lord Jesus, you thirst for love on the Cross. Through the prayers of St Teresa of Calcutta, give us eyes to see you in the poor, hands to serve you, and hearts that do small things with great love. Amen.

points: 10 September 1946, on a train to Darjeeling.
Kalighat, abandoned children, lepers, the dying.
Jesus' thirst for love and souls (John 19:28).
Years of interior darkness, lived with a smile.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, St Teresa of Calcutta, Mother Teresa, is known all over the world. Yet her greatness was in very small things done with great love.

Agnes Bojaxhiu came from Skopje to India in 1929 as a Loreto sister and taught for many years in Kolkata. On 10 September 1946, travelling by train to Darjeeling, she heard what she called a call within the call: to serve Christ in the poorest of the poor. In 1950 she founded the Missionaries of Charity.

She opened a home for the dying at Kalighat, homes for abandoned children, the sick and lepers. In every chapel of her congregation are written the words of Jesus on the Cross: I thirst (John 19:28). She believed that Jesus thirsts for our love, and that we satisfy His thirst by loving Him in the poor.

After her death we learned that for decades she lived in deep interior darkness, without feeling God's presence, yet she kept smiling and serving. Her faith was not a feeling; it was a choice. Let us ask her to help us do small things with great love, and to remain faithful even in darkness.

opts.a: In the light of the Word: I thirst
points: On the Cross Jesus said: I thirst (John 19:28).
I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink (Matthew 25:35).
homily: Dear friends, among the last words of Jesus on the Cross was: I thirst (John 19:28). Mother Teresa placed these words beside the crucifix in every chapel of her congregation. She believed that Jesus thirsts not only for water but for love and for souls.

At the well of Samaria Jesus said to a woman: give me a drink (John 4:7). The Son of God asks for our love. He waits for it, as a beggar waits. Mother Teresa answered that request every day in prayer and in service.

Jesus said: I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink (Matthew 25:35). In the dying man on the street, the leper and the abandoned child, Mother Teresa saw Jesus in what she called His distressing disguise. When she gave them water, she gave it to Christ.

And Jesus also said: let anyone who is thirsty come to me; out of the believer's heart shall flow rivers of living water (John 7:37–38). Mother Teresa could serve so much because she drank first from Christ in the Eucharist and adoration. Let us do the same: receive Him at the {Q}, then give Him to others.

opts.a: For young people and families: love begins at home
points: The unloved in our own homes.
A smile is the beginning of love.
homily: Dear families, when people asked Mother Teresa how they could help her work, she often said: love begins at home. Before going to Kolkata, find your own Kolkata: the lonely, the forgotten, the unloved in your own family.

She said that the greatest poverty in the West is loneliness and the feeling of being unwanted. That poverty exists in our homes too: an elderly parent who no one talks to, a teenager who feels misunderstood, a spouse who feels taken for granted. Give them time and attention.

She also said: we cannot all do great things, but we can do small things with great love. Washing dishes, helping with homework, listening to a sad friend, visiting a sick neighbour: these are not small if done with love.

Young people, Mother Teresa said that a smile is the beginning of love. Smile at your parents, your siblings, the person no one notices in class. And pray every day, even briefly, because she said the fruit of prayer is faith, and the fruit of faith is love, and the fruit of love is service.

martindeporres.t: Dominican lay brother of Lima, servant of the poor and the sick
word: Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me.
Matthew 25:40
life: Martin was born in Lima, Peru, in 1579, the son of a Spanish nobleman, Juan de Porres, and Ana Velázquez, a freed Black woman from Panama. His father at first did not acknowledge him, and as a boy of mixed race Martin knew poverty and contempt. He was apprenticed to a barber-surgeon and learned to dress wounds and prepare medicines.

At about fifteen he asked to join the Dominican priory of the Holy Rosary in Lima. Because of the racial laws of the time he was received first only as a lay helper; in 1603 he was allowed to make his vows as a lay brother. He served as barber, gardener and infirmarian, cared for sick friars and for the poor of the city, founded a home for abandoned children and shared food each day with hundreds of hungry people.

He was a friend of St Rose of Lima and of St Juan Macías. He died on 3 November 1639, and the whole city came to his funeral. Pope St John XXIII canonised him in 1962; he is honoured as a patron of social justice and of people of mixed race.
lessons: Humility is strength
Martin accepted the lowest work without bitterness and so became free to love everyone.
Charity without borders
He served Spaniards, Africans and Indigenous people alike, rich and poor, people and even animals.
Prayer and work together
His long nights of prayer before the Blessed Sacrament were the source of his tireless service by day.
stories: Martin is usually shown holding a broom. He called himself a poor slave and gladly swept the priory, seeing even small tasks as service to Christ.
A popular story says that when the friars wanted to poison the mice in the linen room, Martin led the mice out to the garden and fed them there, and they did no more harm.
martindeporres.prayer: Lord God, you led St Martin de Porres by the path of humility to heavenly glory. Help us to follow his example of charity, so that we may serve Christ in the poor and the sick. Amen.

points: Martin swept floors and called himself a poor slave. Humility made him free to love everyone without pride or bitterness.
Whatever you did to the least of my family you did to me (Matthew 25:40). Martin saw Christ in the sick, the poor, the abandoned child.
Spaniard, African, Indigenous: Martin served all. Ask: whom do I quietly exclude?
homily: Dear friends, today we honour a man the world once looked down upon. Martin de Porres was born poor, of mixed race, unacknowledged by his father. The Dominicans at first would accept him only as a helper. Yet today the whole Church calls him a saint.

Martin never fought for status. He took the broom, the basin and the bandage, and through them he served Christ. Jesus said that whatever we do to the least of his brothers and sisters, we do to him (Matthew 25:40). Martin believed it literally: the sick friar, the beggar at the gate, the abandoned child were Christ himself.

His charity crossed every line his society had drawn: race, class, even the line between people and animals. In a world still divided by colour, caste and status, Martin asks us: whom do I keep at a distance? This week choose one humble task no one wants, and do it with love for Christ. Amen.

charlesborromeo.t: Cardinal Archbishop of Milan, reformer after the Council of Trent
word: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
John 10:11
life: Charles Borromeo was born in 1538 in the castle of Arona on Lake Maggiore, into a noble family. When his uncle became Pope Pius IV in 1559, Charles, only twenty-one, was called to Rome and made a cardinal and the Pope's secretary of state.
